en.title: Reading a menu
en.summary: The sections of a menu, ways of cooking and common descriptions of dishes.

paragraphs: A menu is written in a compact style full of cooking words. In this lesson you will learn to read the sections, to understand the descriptions and to ask the waiter for help.
A guest is looking at the menu in a pub restaurant in Oxford.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.text: What is the dish of the day?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: It is roast beef with vegetables and gravy.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: It is a brown sauce made from meat juices.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: That is a mushroom pie, served with potatoes and peas.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Quite large. Most people can't finish it.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.text: Then I will try the beef.

paragraphs: **1. Past participles describe dishes.** Grilled, roasted, fried and baked tell how the food was cooked and are used before nouns or after be. See Introduction to Grammar: Verbs and verb phrases.
**2. With, without and served with add details.** They connect the main item to the rest of the dish. See Introduction to Grammar: Prepositions and conjunctions.

PhraseExample

in a sauce offish in a sauce of cream

items: A menu has starters, mains, desserts and drinks.
Special means a dish not on the usual menu; the dish of the day changes daily.
A portion is the amount served to one person.
Vegetarian dishes are often marked with a V.

paragraphs: British menus list the price next to each dish, and a service charge may be added to the final bill. In the United States the menu price does not include tax or the tip.
